Compute Significance from Permutation Results

Source: R/significance.R
compute_significance.Rd

Adds permutation p-values, a null envelope, and a whole-curve test to a kernelcomm_result.

compute_significance(
  result,
  method = c("permutation", "moment", "auto"),
  moment_dist = c("gamma", "saddlepoint", "edgeworth", "normal"),
  alternative = c("greater", "less", "two.sided"),
  alpha = 0.05,
  envelope_level = 0.95,
  estimator = c("add_one", "paper"),
  supremum = TRUE,
  sup_standardize = TRUE
)

Arguments

result

Object of class kernelcomm_result

method

Character. "permutation", "moment", or "auto".

moment_dist

Character, how moments become a tail probability. "gamma" (default) matches three moments with a shifted gamma and was the only method with no anti-conservative failures in calibration. "saddlepoint" is better founded and excellent under strong skew but measured worse on near-symmetric real data; treat it as experimental. "edgeworth" and "normal" are provided for comparison and are not recommended: both fail badly in the deep tail under skew.

alternative

Character. "greater" (default, the manuscript's one-tailed upper test), "less", or "two.sided".

alpha

Significance threshold for the significant slot.

envelope_level

Coverage of the null envelope, e.g. 0.95 for the 2.5th to 97.5th percentiles of the permutation distribution. Independent of alpha.

estimator

Character. "add_one" for \((r+1)/(n+1)\) or "paper" for \(r/n\).

supremum

Logical. Also compute the whole-curve supremum test.

sup_standardize

Logical. When TRUE (default), the supremum is taken over deviations standardised by the permutation standard deviation at each bandwidth, so every bandwidth contributes comparably. When FALSE, raw deviations are used, which follows the manuscript literally but is dominated by whichever bandwidth has the largest scale.

Value

The same object with these slots populated: p_values, z_scores, perm_mean, perm_sd, null_lower, null_upper, significant, and when supremum = TRUE, sup_statistic and sup_p_value.

Tail direction

The default is "greater", a one-tailed upper test, matching the companion manuscript: "counting the number of permutations greater than the observed (one tailed) and dividing by the total number of permutations".

This is a corrected default rather than a changed one. The previous version defaulted to "two.sided" but its two-sided branch was empty, so it returned a one-sided upper-tail p-value under a two-sided label. Its "less" option computed 1 - p, which is not a p-value: it can be exactly 0, and it double-counts ties. Both are fixed, and "two.sided" now genuinely tests both tails.

Estimator

"add_one" (default) computes \((r + 1) / (n + 1)\), where \(r\) counts permutations at least as extreme as the observed value. "paper" computes \(r / n\), matching the manuscript literally. "add_one" is the default because \(r / n\) can return exactly 0, which is not a valid p-value estimate and breaks any log transform or FDR procedure downstream; the two differ negligibly except in the far tail, which is exactly where a zero would matter.

Null envelope, not a confidence interval

null_lower and null_upper are quantiles of the permutation distribution. They describe where \(I(h)\) would fall under complete spatial randomness, so the observed curve leaving the band is evidence against the null. They are not a confidence interval for the observed statistic, and were previously named ci_lower/ci_upper and plotted as though they were. The envelope level is now separate from the test threshold, which shared one alpha before, making a 95% band with a 0.01 test impossible.

Why z-scores should not be turned into p-values

z_scores are provided as a comparable effect size, standardising the observed value by the permutation mean and standard deviation. Do not convert them with pnorm(). The permutation null of this statistic is skewed whenever the expression data is skewed, which for zero-inflated single-cell data is the normal case. On a deliberately adversarial example (300 cells, 85% zeros, null skewness 2.4) a normal approximation returned an upper-tail probability 100 times too small at the 0.0001 level, which would manufacture false positives at exactly the threshold an FDR screen operates on. Use the permutation p-values, or the moment-based methods, which model the skewness.

Permutation or moment based

method = "permutation" (default) uses the permutation distribution. "moment" uses the exact analytical moments of the permutation null, which multiScaleAC computes for free, mapped to a tail probability by moment_dist. "auto" uses moments where the diagnostics say a continuous approximation is trustworthy and permutations elsewhere, recording the choice per bandwidth in p_method.

The moments are exact. Mapping them to a tail probability is an approximation, and the default mapping was selected by measurement against 200,000 permutations rather than by theory; see inst/validation/calibrate_moments.R. Permutations remain the default because they need no such approximation.

See also

adjust_pvalues for multiple-testing correction.

Examples

set.seed(1)
n <- 200
coords <- matrix(runif(2 * n), ncol = 2)
g1 <- rnorm(n)
# gene2 spatially related to gene1, so there is something to detect
sm <- exp(-as.matrix(dist(coords))^2 / (2 * 0.1^2))
g2 <- as.vector(sm %*% g1) / rowSums(sm) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)

res <- multiScaleAC(coords, g1, g2, h = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2), perms = 199)
res <- compute_significance(res)
summary(res)
#>      h   observed    perm_mean     perm_sd  z_score p_value p_adjusted
#> 1 0.05 0.09382030 0.0009127632 0.028477044 3.262542   0.005         NA
#> 2 0.10 0.07257447 0.0005312086 0.015354049 4.692135   0.005         NA
#> 3 0.20 0.03384511 0.0003427827 0.007116575 4.707648   0.005         NA
#>   significant  null_lower null_upper
#> 1        TRUE -0.05190806 0.05263404
#> 2        TRUE -0.02594427 0.03084721
#> 3        TRUE -0.01297075 0.01453864

# Whole-curve significance, rather than one test per bandwidth
res@sup_p_value
#> [1] 0.005
